Computer Networks – Deep Concept Notes 
Data Transmission = Encoding + Errors + Medium
Bits don’t travel as bits—they travel as signals:
• Electrical (copper), light (fiber), radio (wireless) 
More aggressive transmission (higher rate, complex modulation):
• Packs more bits per symbol 
• But becomes fragile to noise
Errors come from:
• Attenuation (signal weakens) 
• Noise/interference 
• Imperfect receivers 
So think:
If I push more bits per second, what breaks first—the signal or the receiver’s ability to decode?
Bandwidth vs Throughput = Pipe vs Actual Flow
Bandwidth is a ceiling. Throughput is what you really get.
Why throughput < bandwidth:
• Protocol overhead (headers, ACKs) 
• Retransmissions (loss) 
• Idle times (waiting/backoff) 
• Congestion (queues) 
Hidden effect:
• Even with zero loss, handshakes and ACK pacing reduce throughput. 
So think:
What fraction of time am I actually sending useful data?
Latency = Multiple Delays Add Up
Total delay =
Propagation + Transmission + Processing + Queueing

• Propagation: distance / signal speed (physics) 
• Transmission: packet size / link rate (serialization) 
• Processing: router handling 
• Queueing: waiting behind other packets (variable, often dominant) 
Key insight:
• In lightly loaded networks → propagation dominates 
• In busy networks → queueing dominates 
So think:
Is my delay fixed (distance) or variable (congestion)?
Propagation Delay = The Unavoidable Floor
• Speed ~ 2 × 108m/s in fiber 
• Long links → large round-trip times (RTT) 
Implication:
• ACK-based protocols waste time over long distances 
So think:
Why does stop-and-wait perform terribly over satellite links?
Transmission Delay = Serialization Cost
Time to put bits onto the wire:
𝑇𝑡𝑥 =
packet size
link rate
• Large packets → better efficiency (less header overhead) 
• But increase latency per packet and loss penalty
So think:
Am I optimizing for bulk transfer or quick responses?
Flow Control = Protect the Receiver
Receiver has finite buffer.

Mechanisms:
• Stop-and-wait 
• Sliding window (receiver advertises window size) 
If sender overruns:
• Buffer overflow → drops → retransmissions 
So think:
Is the bottleneck the receiver’s buffer or the network?
Congestion Control = Protect the Network
Different from flow control:
• Flow control → receiver safety 
• Congestion control → network stability
TCP signals congestion via:
• Loss (timeouts, duplicate ACKs) 
• Increasing RTT (queues building) 
Behavior:
• Increase rate until loss → then back off 
So think:
How does TCP “learn” the safe sending rate without seeing inside routers?
Stop-and-Wait = RTT-Limited Efficiency
Efficiency:
𝜂 ≈
𝑇𝑡𝑥
𝑇𝑡𝑥 + 𝑅𝑇𝑇
If RTT ≫ 𝑇𝑡𝑥:
• Link sits idle most of the time 
So think:
Why is utilization near zero on high-latency links?

Sliding Window = Pipeline the Link
Multiple packets “in flight”:
• Keep link busy while waiting for ACKs 
Window size should match:
• Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP)
BDP = bandwidth × 𝑅𝑇𝑇
So think:
How many packets are needed to fully utilize the link?
Error Detection vs Correction
• Detection (CRC): cheap, reliable detection 
• Correction (FEC): adds redundancy to fix errors 
Trade-off:
• Detection → retransmit (delay) 
• Correction → extra bits (overhead) 
So think:
Is it cheaper to resend or to add redundancy upfront?
Retransmission = Reliability Loop
Triggers:
• Timeout (no ACK) 
• Duplicate ACKs (fast retransmit) 
Side-effects:
• More traffic → more congestion 
• Can create feedback loops (more loss → more retransmit → more loss) 
So think:
When does “fixing loss” actually make the network worse?

Packet Size = Efficiency vs Risk
Large packets:
• High efficiency (low header fraction) 
• But if lost → big retransmission cost 
Small packets:
• Low latency, quick recovery 
• High overhead 
So think:
What packet size minimizes total time under loss?
Fragmentation = Adapt to Smaller MTU
When path MTU < packet size:
• Packet is split → fragments 
Costs:
• Extra headers 
• If one fragment lost → whole packet lost 
• Reassembly complexity 
So think:
Why is Path MTU Discovery preferred over fragmentation?
Subnetting = Structure the Network
Divide address space:
• Reduce broadcast domains 
• Improve routing scalability 
Trade-off:
• More subnets → more routing entries 
• Fewer subnets → larger broadcasts 
So think:

How do you size subnets to balance management and performance?
Routing = Metrics, Not Just Distance
Paths chosen based on:
• Hop count 
• Delay 
• Bandwidth 
• Policy 
Dynamic protocols:
• React to failures/congestion 
So think:
Why can a longer path be faster than a shorter one?
TCP vs UDP = Semantics of Delivery
TCP:
• Reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled 
• Head-of-line blocking 
UDP:
• Unreliable, unordered 
• App controls reliability 
So think:
Is your application sensitive to delay or to loss?
DNS = Caching + Hierarchy
Resolution:
• Local cache → recursive resolver → authoritative server 
Caching:
• Reduces latency and load 
• Can cause stale records

So think:
What happens if DNS cache is outdated during a failover?
HTTP/HTTPS = Request/Response + Overheads
HTTP:
• Stateless requests 
• Headers can be large relative to payload 
HTTPS:
• TLS handshake (extra RTTs) 
• Encryption cost 
Optimizations:
• Keep-alive, HTTP/2 multiplexing 
So think:
When does connection setup dominate total time?
TCP Handshake = Establish State
3-way handshake:
• SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK 
Purpose:
• Synchronize sequence numbers 
• Confirm reachability both ways 
Cost:
• At least 1 RTT before data 
So think:
Why do short-lived connections suffer most from handshake overhead?
Congestion Collapse = Positive Feedback Failure
Too much traffic:
• Loss → retransmissions → more load → more loss

Network spends time resending instead of delivering
TCP fixes:
• Slow start 
• Congestion avoidance 
• Backoff 
So think:
How do you prevent the system from spiraling under load?
Queuing = Where Variability Lives
Queues absorb bursts:
• Short queues → low delay 
• Long queues → high latency (bufferbloat) 
Scheduling matters:
• FIFO vs fair queuing 
So think:
Is your delay dominated by queueing, and can scheduling fix it?
Computer Networks – Real-World Thinking Guide
- Network Design = Requirements → Constraints → Choices
A network is not “designed”—it is constrained into existence:
You start with:
• Number of users 
• Type of traffic (video, IoT, web) 
• Required latency 
Then constraints:
• Budget 
• Geography 
• Infrastructure

So think:
Are you designing for performance, cost, or scalability?
- Topology = Reliability vs Cost
Options:
• Star → simple, but central failure 
• Mesh → reliable, but expensive 
• Tree → scalable, but hierarchical dependency 
Trade-off:
More connections → more reliability → more cost
So:
How many failures can your system tolerate?
- Centralized vs Distributed Systems
Centralized:
• Easy control 
• Single point of failure 
Distributed:
• More resilient 
• Harder to manage 
So:
Is failure more costly than complexity?
- Latency vs Throughput Trade-off
Optimizing for:
• Low latency → small packets, less buffering 
• High throughput → large packets, batching 
But:
You cannot optimize both fully

So:
Is your system interactive or bulk-transfer?
- Load vs Capacity = Root of Most Problems
If:
• Demand > capacity → congestion 
Symptoms:
• Delay increases 
• Packet loss 
• Throughput drops 
So:
Is your issue due to insufficient capacity or inefficient usage?
- Bottleneck = System Performance Limit
End-to-end performance is limited by:
• Slowest link 
• Slowest processing node 
Even if rest is fast
So:
Where is the slowest component in your path?
- Scalability = Growth Without Collapse
System that works for 10 users:
• May fail for 1000 
Problems:
• Addressing 
• Routing 
• Load 
So:

Does your design degrade gracefully with scale?
- Caching = Speed vs Freshness
Caching reduces:
• Latency 
• Server load 
But introduces:
• Stale data 
So:
Is outdated data acceptable for your application?
- Debugging Networks = Observe, Don’t Guess
When system fails:
Check:
• Is data being generated? 
• Is it reaching the network? 
• Is it getting dropped? 
Common issues:
• Misconfiguration 
• Congestion 
• DNS failures 
So:
Where in the pipeline is the failure happening?
- Packet Loss = Symptom, Not Root Cause
Loss happens due to:
• Congestion 
• Interference 
• Buffer overflow

Fixing loss:
• Requires fixing cause 
So:
Why is the packet being lost—not just that it is lost?
- Retransmissions = Hidden Load
More loss → more retransmission → more traffic
Creates:
• Feedback loop 
So:
Are retransmissions solving or worsening the problem?
- Queue Build-up = Silent Killer
Before failure:
• Delay increases 
Then:
• Packet drops 
Queues hide the problem until it explodes
So:
Is increasing delay warning you of future failure?
Security – Real Thinking
- Security = Confidentiality + Integrity + Availability
Not just encryption:
• Confidentiality → data hidden 
• Integrity → data not altered 
• Availability → system accessible 
So:

Which of these is most critical for your system?
- Encryption = Security vs Cost
Encryption:
• Protects data 
But:
• Adds computation 
• Adds delay 
So:
Is full encryption necessary for all data?
- Authentication = Trust Establishment
Before accepting data:
• Verify identity 
Without it:
• Fake devices 
• Data poisoning 
So:
How do you trust the sender?
- Attack Surface = More Connectivity, More Risk
Every open port:
• Potential entry point 
IoT:
• Often poorly secured 
So:
What unnecessary exposure can you eliminate?

- DDoS = Resource Exhaustion
Attack floods system with traffic
Effect:
• Legitimate users blocked 
So:
Can your system distinguish real users from attackers?
- Security vs Usability
More security:
• More authentication steps 
• More delay 
Less security:
• Easier access 
So:
What level of inconvenience is acceptable?
Web Deployment & Systems
- Client–Server Model = Separation of Roles
Client:
• Requests 
Server:
• Processes 
Scaling issue:
• One server → bottleneck 
So:
How do you distribute load across multiple servers?

- Load Balancing = Distribute Traffic
Multiple servers:
• Share requests 
Benefits:
• Reliability 
• Scalability 
But:
What happens if load balancer fails?
- Stateless vs Stateful Systems
Stateless:
• Easy scaling 
Stateful:
• Personalized 
• Hard to scale 
So:
Where is user state stored?
- CDN = Move Data Closer
Content served from:
• Nearby servers 
Reduces:
• Latency 
So:
Is your delay due to distance or processing?
- TLS/HTTPS = Secure Web Communication
Adds:

• Encryption 
• Handshake overhead 
But ensures:
• Trust 
So:
When does security overhead dominate response time?
- API Design = Efficiency Matters
Frequent small requests:
• High overhead 
Batching:
• Efficient 
So:
Is your communication pattern optimal?
Troubleshooting Mindset
- Always Trace the Path
Data flow:
• Source → Network → Destination 
Find where it breaks
- Check Layers Separately
• Physical → link working? 
• Network → routing correct? 
• Application → service responding? 
Measure, Don’t Assume
Use:

• Ping (latency) 
• Throughput tests 
• Logs 
Reproduce the Problem
• Is it consistent? 
• Under load only? 
• Location-specific? 
Final Thinking Pattern
For any network problem:
1. What is the requirement? 
2. What is the constraint? 
3. What trade-off is being made? 
4. Where is the bottleneck? 
5. What happens under scale or failure? 
Computer Networks Numericals – Conceptual Insights with Practice
1. Transmission vs Propagation Delay
Sample Numerical:
A 2 MB file is transmitted over a 20 Mbps link. The distance between sender and receiver is 2000 km. 
Signal propagation speed = 2 × 108m/s. Compute total delay.
Crux:
Transmission delay depends on data size and link rate, whereas propagation delay depends on distance 
and signal speed.
Relevance:
Important in long-distance communication (e.g., satellite, undersea cables).
Common Mistakes:
• Not converting MB to bits

• Ignoring propagation delay 
• Mixing units (km vs m) 
Variations:
• Compare which delay dominates 
• Change distance or bandwidth 
• Evaluate impact of larger packet size 
2. Bandwidth–Delay Product
Sample Numerical:
A link has bandwidth 100 Mbps and RTT of 50 ms. Compute the bandwidth-delay product.
Crux:
Represents the amount of data that can be “in transit” in the network.
Relevance:
Used for buffer sizing and determining optimal window size in TCP.
Common Mistakes:
• Using one-way delay instead of RTT 
• Unit mismatch (Mbps × ms) 
Variations:
• Compute required window size 
• Compare with given buffer capacity 
• Analyze under-utilization 
3. Stop-and-Wait Efficiency
Sample Numerical:
Packet size = 2000 bits, bandwidth = 2 Mbps, RTT = 40 ms. Compute efficiency.
Crux:
Efficiency decreases significantly when RTT is large compared to transmission time.
Relevance:
Highlights inefficiency in high-latency networks.
Common Mistakes:
• Ignoring ACK delay

• Misinterpreting RTT 
Variations:
• Increase RTT 
• Compare with sliding window 
• Change packet size 
4. Sliding Window
Sample Numerical:
Window size = 8 packets, packet size = 1000 bits, RTT = 40 ms, bandwidth = 1 Mbps. Compute 
throughput.
Crux:
Throughput improves by allowing multiple packets in transit.
Relevance:
Foundation of TCP performance.
Common Mistakes:
• Not relating window size to bandwidth-delay product 
• Incorrect throughput formula 
Variations:
• Find minimum window size for full utilization 
• Compare with Stop-and-Wait 
• Vary RTT 
5. Error Detection (CRC)
Sample Numerical:
Data = 101101, Generator polynomial = 1101. Compute CRC remainder.
Crux:
CRC detects errors using polynomial division.
Relevance:
Widely used in data link layer protocols.
Common Mistakes:
• Errors in binary division

• Misinterpreting remainder 
Variations:
• Check if received data has error 
• Change generator polynomial 
6. Multi-hop Reliability
Sample Numerical:
Each hop has success probability 0.95. For 4 hops, compute end-to-end success probability.
Crux:
Reliability decreases multiplicatively across hops.
Relevance:
Critical in wireless and IoT networks.
Common Mistakes:
• Adding probabilities instead of multiplying 
Variations:
• Add retransmission 
• Increase number of hops 
7. Throughput with Packet Loss
Sample Numerical:
A 10 Mbps link has 15% packet loss. Estimate effective throughput.
Crux:
Packet loss reduces usable throughput.
Relevance:
Seen in congested or wireless networks.
Common Mistakes:
• Ignoring retransmission overhead 
Variations:
• Include retransmission cost 
• Compare TCP vs UDP

8. Queuing and Congestion
Sample Numerical:
Arrival rate = 1200 packets/sec, service rate = 1000 packets/sec. Determine system behavior.
Crux:
If arrival rate exceeds service rate, the queue grows indefinitely.
Relevance:
Core concept in congestion analysis.
Common Mistakes:
• Not checking stability condition 
Variations:
• Compute queue growth over time 
• Reduce arrival rate 
9. Fragmentation
Sample Numerical:
Packet size = 3000 bytes, MTU = 1000 bytes. Determine number of fragments.
Crux:
Large packets must be divided to fit network constraints.
Relevance:
Important in IP networks.
Common Mistakes:
• Ignoring header overhead 
Variations:
• Compute total transmitted size 
• Compare with path MTU discovery 
10. Subnetting
Sample Numerical:
Given 192.168.10.0/24, design subnets for 30 hosts each.
Crux:
Efficient allocation of IP addresses.

Relevance:
Enterprise network design.
Common Mistakes:
• Incorrect host calculation 
• Confusing network and broadcast addresses 
Variations:
• Different host requirements 
• Identify subnet mask 
11. Load vs Capacity
Sample Numerical:
200 devices send 500 bytes every second over a 1 Mbps link. Check if network is overloaded.
Crux:
System fails when demand exceeds capacity.
Relevance:
Scalability analysis.
Common Mistakes:
• Ignoring protocol overhead 
Variations:
• Increase number of devices 
• Reduce bandwidth 
12. TCP Throughput
Sample Numerical:
RTT = 80 ms, packet loss = 0.02. Analyze throughput trend.
Crux:
TCP throughput depends on both delay and loss.
Relevance:
Internet performance.
Common Mistakes:
• Ignoring RTT impact

Variations:
• Change loss rate 
• Compare wired vs wireless 
13. DNS Delay
Sample Numerical:
DNS resolution requires 4 queries, each taking 25 ms. Compute total delay.
Crux:
Multiple lookups increase delay.
Relevance:
Web browsing performance.
Common Mistakes:
• Ignoring caching 
Variations:
• Add cache 
• Reduce number of queries 
14. HTTP Transfer Time
Sample Numerical:
A 2 MB file is downloaded over a 10 Mbps link with RTT = 40 ms. Compute total time including 
connection setup.
Crux:
Total time includes handshake + data transfer.
Relevance:
Web performance optimization.
Common Mistakes:
• Ignoring RTT 
• Missing handshake delay 
Variations:
• Persistent connections 
• HTTPS vs HTTP

15. TCP Handshake
Sample Numerical:
RTT = 60 ms. Compute time required before first data byte arrives.
Crux:
Handshake introduces fixed delay.
Relevance:
Short transactions suffer most.
Common Mistakes:
• Forgetting handshake phase 
Variations:
• Add TLS handshake 
• Compare persistent connections 
16. Routing Path Selection
Sample Numerical:
Path A: 4 hops × 8 ms each
Path B: 6 hops × 5 ms each
Determine faster path.
Crux:
Shortest path is not always fastest.
Relevance:
Routing decisions in networks.
Common Mistakes:
• Ignoring per-hop delay differences 
Variations:
• Add congestion 
• Add bandwidth constraints 
17. Congestion Analysis
Sample Numerical:
Link capacity = 20 Mbps, offered load = 30 Mbps. Analyze system behavior.

Crux:
Overload leads to congestion collapse.
Relevance:
Network stability.
Common Mistakes:
• Assuming linear degradation 
Variations:
• Add queue size 
• Reduce load 
18. Packet Size Trade-off
Sample Numerical:
Compare transmission time for 500-byte and 1500-byte packets over 5 Mbps link.
Crux:
Trade-off between efficiency and delay.
Relevance:
Protocol design.
Common Mistakes:
• Ignoring overhead 
Variations:
• Add loss probability 
• Compare efficiency 
19. Multi-hop Delay
Sample Numerical:
A packet passes through 5 routers, each adding 3 ms delay. Transmission delay = 4 ms. Compute total 
delay.
Crux:
Delay accumulates across hops.
Relevance:
End-to-end performance.
Common Mistakes:

• Missing one delay component 
Variations:
• Add propagation delay 
• Add queueing delay 
20. Load Balancing
Sample Numerical:
4 servers share 1200 requests/sec equally. Compute load per server.
Crux:
Load distribution prevents bottlenecks.
Relevance:
Web system design.
Common Mistakes:
• Assuming equal distribution always 
Variations:
• Uneven distribution 
• Server failure scenario
